summary: Explains what it means for a domain name to be reserved for special use, when that is appropriate, and the procedure for doing it. It establishes an IANA registry of such names and seeds it with entries for some already established special domain names. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Some names in the internet phone book are held back for special jobs, like reserved parking spots. This memo says how a spot gets reserved and keeps a public list.

questions: how to reserve a special-use domain name
what is a special-use domain name

subtitle: When a domain name may be reserved for special handling, how to ask for it, and the first names on the list.

tldr.problem: Some domain names, such as example.com or invalid, are meant to behave differently from ordinary names, but RFC 2606 never said whether software should treat them differently, or how.
tldr.mechanism: Any new special name needs a Standards Action or IESG Approval document that answers seven questions about how users, software, DNS servers and registrars must treat it. IANA records the name in a new registry, seeded with the private-address reverse domains, test, localhost, invalid and the example names.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6761 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1918 and RFC 2606, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

facts.label: Seeded names
facts.value: Private reverse domains, test, localhost, invalid, example names

sections.title: Why Special Names Need Rules
sections.content:
Some IP addresses are treated specially by network software. Examples are the multicast range 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 and the local host address 127.0.0.1. Analogously, the DNS already had reserved names such as example.com., example.net., example.org. and anything under the pseudo top-level domain invalid..

The gap was that RFC 2606 did not say whether implementations should treat such names differently, or in what way. RFC 6761 fills that gap: it specifies when special treatment is appropriate and what form it takes.
sections.eli5: Some names were already set aside, like a roped-off seat at a show, but nobody wrote down what the ushers should do about it. This memo writes it down.

sections.title: When a Name Deserves to Be Special
sections.content:
A name is a candidate when it has special properties that affect how hardware and software handle it, and those properties apply on every network the implementation may be connected to. The RFC compares this to IP multicast: 224.0.0.1 is always the "all hosts" address, and that is not a local decision.

If declaring a name special would change no implementation, the name is probably not special in any material way, and the normal DNS delegation mechanisms should be used. The RFC states that reserving a Special-Use Domain Name is not a mechanism for circumventing normal domain name registration processes.

The RFC also explains why this is the IETF's job. The IETF is responsible for protocol rules, and ICANN allocates the names those rules make possible. A name that is guaranteed to return NXDOMAIN is only useful if that guarantee holds by protocol on all networks, including private ones that ICANN has no jurisdiction over.
sections.eli5: A name only gets a reserved seat if every theatre in the world has to treat it the same way. If nothing would change, it is just an ordinary ticket.

sections.title: The Procedure and the Seven Questions
sections.content:
If special handling of a name is required to implement some new functionality, an IETF "Standards Action" or "IESG Approval" specification MUST be published. It MUST say how implementations decide that special handling applies, typically by stating that any name ending in a certain suffix gets the special behaviour. This carves off a sub-tree of the DNS namespace.

The specification also MUST answer seven "Domain Name Reservation Considerations", in a subsection of its IANA Considerations section. For each one it says what special treatment, if any, applies. If all seven answers are "none", the name probably does not need reserving.

The seven audiences are: users, application software, name resolution APIs and libraries, caching DNS servers, authoritative DNS servers, DNS server operators, and DNS registries and registrars.

For algorithmically generated names, the document needs to clearly identify the set of generated names that need the special treatment.
sections.eli5: To reserve a name you fill in a form with seven questions, one for each kind of person or program that might meet the name. If every answer is "nothing special", you do not need the reservation.

sections.title: The Initial Registry Entries
sections.content:
The registry starts with the private-address reverse-mapping domains from RFC 1918 and the existing reserved names from RFC 2606. Each is described using the seven questions.

  • Private-address reverse domains (10.in-addr.arpa., 16.172.in-addr.arpa. through 31.172.in-addr.arpa., and 168.192.in-addr.arpa.): results may differ between networks. Caching servers SHOULD answer immediately by default rather than query upstream, with an option, disabled by default, to resolve them upstream.
  • test.: handled much the same way, with immediate negative responses by default.
  • localhost.: users may assume address queries resolve to the IP loopback address. Resolver libraries SHOULD return the loopback address for address queries and negative responses for other query types, without querying a caching server.
  • invalid.: users MAY assume queries always return NXDOMAIN, and resolvers and caching servers SHOULD answer that immediately.
  • example., example.com., example.net., example.org.: reserved for documentation. Software SHOULD NOT treat them as special and caching servers SHOULD resolve them normally.

For every one of these, registries and registrars MUST NOT grant requests to register the names in the normal way. The example names are registered in perpetuity to IANA.
sections.eli5: The first list holds a few names with simple jobs: some always point back at your own computer, some never exist, and some are only for examples in instruction books. Nobody is allowed to buy them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 6761 itself adds little here. It says that any document requesting a Special-Use Domain Name needs to contain its own appropriate Security Considerations section describing the security issues relevant to that special use.
sections.eli5: Anyone who asks for a reserved name has to say what could go wrong with it. This memo only sets that rule.

sections.title: How IANA Records a New Name
sections.content:
IANA has created a registry of Special-Use Domain Names, initially populated with the entries from Section 6.

When a request arrives, IANA should verify, in consultation with the IESG, that the Standards Action or IESG Approval document includes the required "Domain Name Reservation Considerations" section covering the seven categories. If IANA and the IESG decide that special handling is appropriate, IANA should record the name and a reference to the specification that documents it.
sections.eli5: The keeper of the list checks that the form is filled in properly, and if it is, writes the new name in the book.
